rv.q: This struggle defeats the drama: Schmidt has written them as if they're protagonists of two different plays, from two different genres.
Unfortunately at this point most in the audience will be hoping that the play itself will soon come to a merciful end.
The Disappear quickly reveals itself as bitter and thin, its in-crowd jokes sucking oxygen from the room.
The play's messages about marriage, art and other big questions are buried in a production that is nearly unbearable to watch.
The Disappear echoes the Chekhovian interweaving of comedy and tragedy, capturing the absurdity of human connection against a backdrop of impending cataclysm.
Though entertaining, Erica Schmidt’s The Disappear is a patchy examination of artistic and personal sacrifices.
The Disappear probably won’t leave you quaking with laughter or shaking with grim recognition of your own frail mortality.
The playwright never seems to find a coherent tone, or even theme, for the play, which she stages with the sort of self-indulgence demonstrated by so many writers directing their own work.
The world may be falling apart, but seeing The Disappear would be part of any good plan around disaster.
A pleasant entertainment, especially if you enjoy how good actors can elevate a script.
Nevertheless, for all its flaws, The Disappear (an awkward title) is a fun show, the kind of marital comedy no one writes for the stage anymore but once populated Broadway.
She's assembled actors capable of making us care. If only the play would let them.
The audience for The Disappear will have checked out long before the final blackout.
One leaves admiring individual moments while wishing the play itself had disappeared a little sooner, or else arrived with greater clarity about what, exactly, it wanted to be.
